item.title: Oh My GOD.
item.content:encoded:
This may have cleared the awful headcanons of others, but only worsened mine.

Many of us are aware of the sheer number of reality-altering SCPs contained, and the existence of those that are classified as "safe" and even used for menial tasks…

The final lines: "The young doctor felt the anxiety there, but beneath it was something else. The dread had vanished, but the fear remained, quiet and looming.
He turned off the monitors, gathered his notes, and left the room." sealed my headcanon for me -

Perhaps something unfathomably horrible is actually happening to "Katherine", but with the large metal plates obscuring direct view of 110-Montauk and the potential usage of a reality-altering SCP to alter what Montgomery (and others) saw on the feed - those not directly involved in the undertaking/directing of the procedure may feel a sense of relief - a necessary one that motivates them to continue working on their assignment with 231-7 to ensure efficiency and adequate support.

Am I just pessimistic? Perhaps.
But that doesn't change the plausibility of my headcanon.
110-Montauk is just as horrifying (or perhaps more so) than we imagined.
Montgomery is simply made ignorant of that fact so that he may carry out his job without potentially disruptive negative emotions clouding his mind.

And this fact makes the whole scenario even more horrifying.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I totally get the hype and praise for this - the writing is great, and it's completely successful at what it sets out to do, and deserves all the upvotes, and I upvoted it.

That said, while I can appreciate this, I prefer my 231 straight up. I feel like the controversy over the sexual implications in the original article misses the point, and, anyway, it seems like a failure of imagination to think the mind-shriveling awfulness of 110-Montauk could be anything as simple as "they're raping her." But to me that's just a distraction - to me, the procedure itself is irrelevant.

The point is that 110-Montauk, whether sexual or not, is something bad. It's so bad that the Foundation has a problem with people deciding they'd rather let the world end than keep doing it. How do you handle that? To sidestep the dilemma by saying it's all for show is a neat story device, but in this particular case it feels like cheating.

item.content:encoded:
I'm of two minds about this. 110-Montauk has, up to this point, made 231 the most horrifying, terror ridden SCP possible. It served as a graphic illustration of how far the Foundation was willing to go to protect the world, and the implication that it was too monstrous to fully document, along with what little was implied to push the imagination a certain way, was masterful horror writing at it's best.

On the one hand, it's something of a relief to know that Montauk does not involve the terrible things that ran through my mind upon first reading 231. On the other hand, after reading this, 231 has been neutered of most of it's terror aspect and become just another keter level SCP, no scarier than 682.

It's a great story, and I enjoyed the read, but in my opinion you just broke one of the best SCPs.

item.title: Re: Giant Gaping Plot Holes (Fear Alone)
item.content:encoded:
The other thing about this is that we're to assume from 231 that Scarlet King, being the harbringer of destruction that it is, isn't just rewarding 110-Montauk with compliance out of the goodness of its heart. The point is that it's kept at bay by the fear and association with horrible acts - they're like the wall keeping it from being born; either revulsion of the Scarlet King exists, or the Scarlet King does. I guess the phrasing in the Tale is different, but like…even if it knew that everything that was happening was fake, would it really be able to do anything about it, when there's thousands and thousands of agents going around living with the debilitating fear that they have participated in 110-Montauk multiple times?

As far as the Tales about agents who refuse to take amnestics, just because the Foundation is unwilling to rape a child doesn't mean they're not willing to do shitty things. They're a morally grey organization after all. They probably have to plant false memories or delusions in agents' heads every once in a while in order to continue keeping the creature at bay.

Anyway, enough meta, I absolutely love this Tale and theory, it completely redeems 231 and the entire wiki for me.
Yes.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
See, the thing about the SCP-231 file is that it's intentionally vague. We know that SCP-231-7 is a young girl, who is pregnant, and something is done to her to prevent a potential XK scenario that is most effective around the third or fourth time after amnestics. That's it. Nothing is said about demons or elder gods, or even rules.
Procedure 110-Montauk is intentionally left undefined.
Procedure 110-Montauk is described as being ugly.
Procedure 110-Montauk is a secret.
People tend to get interested in ugly secrets.
People start looking into things they're interested in.
This tale provides a nice happy answer to an ugly secret.
People like nice happy answers.
When people find a nice happy answer to something they're interested in, they consider it 'resolved' and move on.
People don't look deeper when they move on.
The Foundation knows how people work.
The Foundation doesn't want people to look deeper into Procedure 110-Montauk.
Why?

It's a secret.

item.content:encoded:
There I am, looking for some high-rated tales not yet translated. There it is, lying around and waiting to be seen.
Translated and upvoted enthusiastically. There are some points to discuss though.

First off, the build-up of fear in Montgomery seems… too deliberate. It's like half of the tale is spent showing us how he gets more and more anxious. This discussion indicates that some people like it, but to each his own, I guess.

Second, the clock seems to be migrating around the room. Initially it is said to be hanging on a wall, later it's above an observation window.

Targus' description is given gradually. He's not being described as tanned or old initially, and I don't like when my idea of a character has to change near the end of a tale.

Lastly, "debrief new assignments" is kinda what he does. As far as I know, debriefing is usually done after a mission. You probably wanted to say "brief".

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm someone who's always been uncomfortable with the discussion around SCP-231 (though I like the SCP itself) because it felt far too much like taking very grave subjects that have particular relevance for me and my childhood and turning them into, idk, a thrill? Sure, not an approving thrill, but a thrill nonetheless. I was thankful to DrClef for emphasising what Montauk was not, and I'm also thankful to you for creating something that has compassion at its heart.

Much SCP writing is done as a one-up over other SCPs, in my opinion - it's done to scare and horrify, of course, and that means the evil of the Foundation is up to 11 all over the place. Sometimes, though, I think the most powerful SCPs are the ones which emphasise that the Foundation is made up of human beings, occasionally flawed in their ability to empathise with creatures and beings which don't understand or value empathy, but also willing to find solutions like this. Personally, I don't see much point in a Foundation so indifferent to morality that it would maintain the world beyond the point that it's worth saving.

Whether or not you like dark Foundation or not, though, this answer to the Montauk question subverts expectations, and it's worth it for that alone.

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
I'm going to preface my opinion by praising this tale. Excellently written. Provides an interesting twist, and a lighthearted alternative, to this masterpiece of horror. Holds the reader in blissful suspense for what we have been told is really going on, and then flips you on your head. Enjoyed this wholeheartedly.

Now, onto the part of my opinion that makes me a terrible person. While I love how this provides a plausible alternative to the awfulness that is Procedure 110-Montauk, my headcanon refuses to allow me to believe that the procedure is anything less that the disturbing event most people believe it to be. SCP-231-7 has always been the shining example of the Foundation's rock-solid belief that "the ends justify the means", at least to me, and I feel that sense of duty is diminished with this tale. It gives people the ability to shy away from the terrible reality of what is happening in that room.

But, this could just be the heavily opinionated rant of a deranged individual who hates happiness and delights in filth. While I cannot believe this to be the true Procedure 110-Montauk, it is still amazing and had me on the edge of my seat… +1.

That's got the sappy down, but nope, nothing like this one did. I think it's the years I've spent seeing references to this here and there and thinking "that poor girl". And then… she's being read bedtime stories. Ones I still like even, and I'm a few months shy of 30.

All the horrible things I've imagined could hide behind the [redacted] — they are themselves the containment. Not what's being done to her, but how people react to that ambiguity. And that? That the Foundation would spread massive disinformation? Totally believable. That everyone, in universe and on site, would assume the worst? Well, we did/do. That the Foundation is actually being quite nice to her since the disinformation campaign is the real containment? That right there is hope.

This needs the horror built up around 231-7 for it to work, and it gets all meta and makes me go all sappy.

Idk, blame the nesting instinct? Mine's on high drive after acknowledging I'm probably not reproducing and getting a tortoise (he'll probably outlive me, is adorable, bath time and little yawns and decorating and no teenage years! …yeah, see? Nesting.)
